chunks.text: Dar al-Islam means the 'house' or 'abode of Islam.' It refers to the vast belt of Afro-Eurasian lands where Islam was the dominant faith and shaped law, learning, trade, and daily life from c. 1200 to c. 1450.

By 1200 the Islamic world had no single ruler, yet it remained a unified civilization. It was politically fragmented into competing states but culturally and religiously whole, bound by a shared faith, the Arabic language of scholarship, common law, pilgrimage routes, and trade networks.

Ibn Battuta was a Moroccan legal scholar who traveled across Dar al-Islam for nearly thirty years beginning in the 1320s, journeying from North Africa to Arabia, Central Asia, India, and beyond. His travels show how a shared religion, law, and the Arabic language connected the far-flung Islamic world.

The Abbasid Caliphate, founded in 750 CE and centered on Baghdad, had once governed a vast empire but by 1200 had fragmented. The caliph remained respected as a religious figurehead but no longer held real political or military power.

Turkic peoples were nomadic groups from Central Asia who converted to Islam and possessed formidable military skill, especially as cavalry. New Islamic states in this era were repeatedly founded or dominated by Turkic peoples.

The Seljuk Turks were a Turkic group who took over the Abbasid heartland in the eleventh century. Their leader took the title sultan and held real power, while the Abbasid caliph was kept on as a religious symbol.

In this period the caliph claimed religious legitimacy as a figurehead, while the sultan held the army and ran the actual government. A simple way to remember the distinction: the caliph blessed, but the sultan ruled.

The Mamluk Sultanate ruled Egypt and Syria from 1250 to 1517. The Mamluks were originally enslaved soldiers, often Turkic or Circassian boys, who were purchased young, converted to Islam, trained as elite warriors, and then seized power for themselves.

At the Battle of Ain Jalut in 1260, the Mamluks of Egypt halted the advancing Mongols, inflicting one of the first major defeats the Mongols ever suffered. The Mamluks also finished off the last Crusader strongholds in the region.

The Delhi Sultanate was a Muslim state founded by Turkic and Afghan rulers that brought Islamic political rule to northern India beginning in 1206. It is a key example of Turkic-led Islamic expansion into South Asia.

The House of Wisdom was a center of learning in Baghdad founded by earlier Abbasid caliphs, where scholars translated Greek, Persian, and Indian works into Arabic. This translation movement preserved ancient Mediterranean philosophy and science that had been lost to western Europe.

Muslim scholars preserved the works of ancient Greek thinkers such as Aristotle, Plato, Euclid, and Galen by translating them into Arabic. For centuries, the best way to read many of these classical texts was in Arabic translation.

Al-Khwarizmi (c. 780–850) was a mathematician who developed the systematic methods now called algebra; the word 'algebra' comes from the Arabic 'al-jabr' in the title of his book. He also helped popularize the decimal, place-value number system, including zero, that Muslim scholars had learned from India.

The place-value number system with the digits 0 through 9, including the concept of zero, originated in India. Muslim scholars adopted it and transmitted it to Europe, where it became known as 'Arabic numerals' even though its ultimate origin was Indian, eventually replacing Roman numerals.
Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna (c. 980–1037), wrote the Canon of Medicine, an encyclopedia of medical knowledge that was used as a standard textbook in Europe for roughly five hundred years.

Ibn Rushd, known in Europe as Averroes, wrote influential commentaries on the philosophy of Aristotle. His work later shaped European thinkers and helped reintroduce Aristotle into European universities.

Nasir al-Din al-Tusi (1201–1274) was a Persian polymath who made major advances in trigonometry and astronomy and built a great observatory at Maragha, showing that the Islamic golden age of learning continued into this period.

'A'isha al-Ba'uniyya was a fifteenth-century scholar from Damascus who became one of the most prolific female writers of the pre-modern Arabic world, composing celebrated works of Sufi poetry and religious devotion. She shows that scholarship in Dar al-Islam was not exclusively male.

Dar al-Islam acted as a hub where knowledge was preserved, synthesized from Greek, Persian, and Indian sources, advanced, and then transferred onward. Much of this learning later passed to Europe and helped lay foundations for the European Renaissance.

Islam spread in this era through three main mechanisms: military expansion by Turkic states, the commercial networks of Muslim merchants, and the preaching of Sufi missionaries. It often expanded more through peaceful trade and missionary work than through conquest.

Muslim merchants dominated key trade arteries such as the Indian Ocean sea lanes, the trans-Saharan caravan routes, and the Silk Roads. Wherever they settled, they brought their faith, married into local communities, and built mosques, so conversion often followed commerce, especially in West Africa, East Africa, and Southeast Asia.

Sufism is a mystical form of Islam whose practitioners, called Sufis, sought a direct, personal experience of God through meditation, poetry, and chanting. Sufi missionaries often blended Islamic teaching with existing local customs, making the faith accessible and aiding its spread into South Asia and Africa.

From 1200 to 1450 the Islamic world changed politically as the unified Abbasid Caliphate fragmented and power passed to Turkic states, but it maintained continuity through a shared religion, the Arabic language, common law, pilgrimage, and a flourishing scholarly tradition.

In 1258 the Mongols sacked Baghdad and ended the Abbasid line, a dramatic political change in the Islamic world. Despite this, Islam remained the unifying faith and Dar al-Islam continued as a single civilization.

European scholars in the twelfth through fifteenth centuries recovered much lost Greek learning through Arabic translations and commentaries, accessed via Muslim Spain (al-Andalus), Sicily, and Mediterranean trade and Crusader contacts. In this way Dar al-Islam served as a bridge that helped make the European Renaissance possible.
